title: A modern army
hookLine: he trains his army with European officers alongside Sikh generals

cards: A parade ground outside Lahore, early morning. Rows of foot soldiers in matching jackets march in step to drums, turn on one command, and fire together. Officers shout orders in a mix of languages.

Some are Punjabi chiefs whose families rode with the misls. Some have come from very far away, from France and Italy, men who learned soldiering in the wars of Europe. The misls fought as bands of horsemen.

teach.b: Ranjit Singh had a problem. The misl way of fighting, fast riders striking and vanishing, had won the Punjab. But across the river he had seen the British, with trained infantry and artillery that fought as one machine.
He could ignore that, or learn from it. He learned.

He built new regiments of infantry and artillery drilled in the European way, and hired European officers to train them, among them Jean-Baptiste Ventura and Jean-François Allard, who had served in Napoleon's armies.
Accounts say he set them conditions: to respect Sikh ways in his lands and, some sources say, not to eat beef or smoke. They taught drill and gunnery, and some led the new regiments on campaign.
But the Maharaja kept command in his own hands, and his great campaigns were led by his own generals, Sikh and Punjabi. Learning from outside is not new in Sikh history.

teach.h: SAINTS OF EVERY BACKGROUND IN THE GRANTH.
teach.b: The Guru Granth Sahib holds the Gurus' hymns beside those of saints from very different backgrounds: Kabir the weaver, Ravidas the leatherworker, Namdev the tailor, and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi.

In Sikh telling, those words were placed in the scripture for what they say, not for where their writers came from, and Guru Arjan gathered them into the book himself. The parade ground was a long way from the Granth.
But the habit underneath was the same: truth and skill can come through anyone.

how: Sikh histories remember Ranjit Singh's army, trained in part by European officers and led by Sikh and Punjabi generals; the Guru Granth Sahib includes the hymns of the Gurus alongside those of saints from many backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim.

games.q: you've watched the British drill across the river: infantry and guns that fight as one. your army is fast riders. what do you do?
o: ignore it: riders won the Punjab.
hire officers who know that drill, and keep command with your own generals.
hand the whole army over to the foreigners.
games.why: he hired European officers to train new regiments, set them conditions, and kept command in his own hands, with his own Sikh and Punjabi generals.

practice: Think of someone you don't usually learn from: someone much younger, from a very different background, a coworker you find irritating, a stranger you overheard once.
Let one thing they know how to do, or one way they see, come to mind, and hold it with curiosity rather than judgment, Waheguru on the breath out if you pray.
